items.headline: Michael Giles, King Crimson's original drummer, dies at 84
items.summary: he died on 23 November, and Robert Fripp's Discipline Global Mobile announced it on 25 November.
items.matters: he played on the 1969 debut "In The Court Of The Crimson King" and had released a new solo album, "Shadows/Solo", earlier in 2026.
items.body:
Michael Giles, the original drummer of English prog-rock titans King Crimson, has died. Discipline Global Mobile, the record label founded by his old bandmate Robert Fripp, shared the news today, confirming that Giles passed away on Nov. 23. He was 84.

Following the addition of multi-instrumentalist Ian McDonald and the departure of Peter Giles, the group morphed into the first incarnation of King Crimson, rounded out by bassist/vocalist Greg Lake and lyricist Peter Sinfield. Michael Giles played on their landmark 1969 debut In The Court Of The Crimson King before leaving the band, although he still contributed to their 1970 follow-up In The Wake Of Poseidon.

Giles briefly formed a duo with fellow former King Crimson member Ian McDonald, releasing the self-titled album McDonald And Giles in 1970. He then transitioned into a successful career as a session musician, working with acts including Steve Winwood, Bryan Ferry, Leo Sayer, Anthony Phillips, Kevin Ayers, Greg Lake, Neil Sedaka, Yvonne Elliman, Rupert Hine, Roger Glover, Francis Monkman, Andy Summers, and the Penguin Cafe Orchestra.

In 2001, Giles released his first solo album, Progress. A year later, he co-founded the 21st Century Schizoid Band, performing material from King Crimson's early period with other ex-members. He released his most recent solo album, Shadows/Solo, earlier this year.

items.headline: The Chicks join Jason Isbell's class action against Suno
items.summary: the complaint amended on 24 November adds 16 plaintiffs, including David Longstreth, Carl Craig, Phil Elverum and Ezra Furman, and targets Suno's v6 models.
items.matters: the suit has no copyright claims. It rests on right-of-publicity laws in 14 states and Puerto Rico plus Illinois' biometric privacy law, and Universal and Sony's separate copyright cases continue.
items.body:
A new group of artists has joined Jason Isbell ‘s proposed class action lawsuit against Suno, according to an amended complaint filed in Boston federal court on Tuesday (November 24).

Those artists include The Chicks (Martie Maguire, Natalie Maines, and Emily Strayer), Dirty Projectors founder David Longstreth, Detroit techno producer Carl Craig, Mount Eerie’s Phil Elverum, and singer-songwriter Ezra Furman.

The surviving spouses of salsa bandleader Willie Colón and Sam & Dave singer Sam Moore have signed on too.

In total, the amended complaint names 16 new plaintiffs. The others are Andrew Choi (St. Lenox), Lydia Loveless, Laurel Massé, Franz Nicolay, William Pollak (Billy Price), Kealiʻi Reichel, and Ike Reilly.

Isbell filed the original suit on August 31 alongside David Lowery, Guy Forsyth, and Eduardo Calle, as reported by MBW at the time.

The case contains no copyright claims. Instead, it accuses Suno of encoding musicians’ identities into its AI models and answering their names with songs, text descriptions, and cover images that evoke them, without consent.

The claims are brought under right-of-publicity laws in 14 US states and Puerto Rico, as well as Illinois’ Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA).

The amended filing comes 21 days after Suno asked the court to dismiss the case. Under federal rules, that was the last day the plaintiffs could amend their complaint without Suno ‘s consent or the court’s permission.

It also argued that the four original plaintiffs lacked standing to pursue claims under the laws of states where none of them lived, including Illinois’ BIPA.

The motion made the same argument about post-mortem right-of-publicity claims, noting that none of the four represented an estate or an heir.

Suno also wanted the BIPA claim dismissed or paused in favor of a separate suit filed in Illinois in October 2025 by songwriter David Woulard.

The new plaintiffs include residents of Illinois, California, New York, Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Washington, Massachusetts, New Jersey, and Hawaii, according to the filing.

By MBW ‘s count, Puerto Rico is now the only jurisdiction named in the complaint without a plaintiff based there.

The filing argues that the named plaintiffs’ claims “encompass” those of a Puerto Rico subclass, because the other states’ laws require plaintiffs to meet “the same or more demanding standards” than Puerto Rico’s.

Julia Colón Craig and Joyce Moore sue as heirs of Colón, who died in February 2026, and Moore, who died in January 2025.

items.headline: PRS for Music signs a licensing deal with Roblox
items.summary: announced 25 November, with royalties to songwriters, composers and publishers starting in 2027.
items.matters: the financial terms are undisclosed, and PRS's March lawsuit against Steam operator Valve over unlicensed music is still running.
items.body:
PRS for Music has signed a licensing agreement with Roblox covering the use of music across the gaming and creation platform.

PRS says it will start distributing royalty payments to songwriters, composers, and publishers in 2027.

That figure was up 12% quarter-over-quarter, but down 9% year-over-year, according to Roblox ‘s Q3 shareholder letter, which attributed the decline to difficult comparisons with the company’s growth in 2025.

“Roblox is far more than a gaming platform; it is where entire communities create, share and play in immersive virtual experiences,” said Dan Gopal, Chief Commercial Officer at PRS for Music.

The deal forms part of a wider effort by PRS to license music use in video games.

In March, the society launched legal action against Steam operator Valve Corporation, alleging that Valve has never obtained a license for PRS members’ music since the store launched in 2003.

The case concerns the “communication to the public” right, which in the UK sits with PRS rather than with individual music publishers.

PRS said at the time that the litigation would continue unless Valve agreed to a license covering both past and future use of PRS members’ music.

In a May 2025 op-ed for MBW, PRS executives George Rose and Graham Best called for “a clear and decisive shift away from buyouts, and towards a consistent royalty model” for music in games.

The pair pointed to Roblox and Fortnite, arguing that licenses from collection societies could allow such platforms to expand the range of music they offer.

Earlier this month, Symphonic struck an agreement to bring “hundreds of thousands of curated songs” to the Roblox Creator Store, according to the distributor.

In July, Roblox partnered with Too Lost, adding thousands of tracks distributed by the company to the Roblox Creator Store.

In 2024, Roblox struck a deal with DistroKid that let independent artists opt in to making their music available on the platform via an invite-only beta.

Artists who took part granted Roblox developers rights to use their music “on a gratis basis,” according to an opt-in form seen by MBW at the time.

Those artists were also required to own 100% of their publishing rights and not be registered with a performing rights organization such as ASCAP or BMI.

In June 2021, a group of music publishers sued Roblox via the National Music Publishers’ Association (NMPA) for more than USD $200 million in damages, alleging copyright infringement.

items.body:
The complaint, obtained and first reported by MBW, was filed on Tuesday (November 24) in the US District Court for the Central District of California.

One section of the filing is headed with the claim that Walmart is a “serial infringer,” and lists intellectual property disputes involving the retailer stretching back to the late 1990s.

Among them, according to the complaint, is a USD $6.4 million settlement that Walmart paid to resolve a lawsuit brought by Tommy Hilfiger, which alleged that Walmart sold counterfeit Hilfiger-brand T-shirts.

The plaintiffs say they own the copyright to all images and video recordings made at Coachella under the festival’s ticket terms, and argue that Walmart either breached that contract or induced someone else to breach it.

In April 2023, the complaint alleges, Walmart’s store in La Quinta, California, used signage “copied directly from Plaintiffs’ line-up posters from prior festivals” to promote items including beverage coolers and folding chairs.

The signage was removed after the plaintiffs sent another cease-and-desist letter to Walmart ‘s General Counsel, according to the complaint.

“In April 2026, undeterred by knowledge at the highest corporate levels that its sale of unlicensed goods bearing the Coachella Marks is wrongful, Walmart again disregarded Plaintiffs’ rights and resumed offering the sale of products at the La Quinta Walmart that displayed the Coachella Marks without Plaintiffs’ approval, license, or authorization,” the complaint alleges.

items.headline: Worth watching this week: The Mosquito Bowl, now on Netflix
items.summary: Peter Berg's World War II drama follows Marines, several of them former football stars, who play a game on Guadalcanal on Christmas Eve 1944, with Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgård and Ray Nicholson.
items.matters: reviews are mixed: TheWrap praises the sound design and cinematography but calls it hard to recommend beyond its target audience, and it arrived on Netflix on 25 November after a limited theatrical run from 30 October.
items.body:
If I’m typing a little slowly today, it’s because I slipped in a pile of excess testosterone and hurt my back after watching Peter Berg ’s “The Mosquito Bowl.” It’s a manly film about manly men pursuing manly pursuits, like football, war and racism. It’s a film where women exist to pack men’s bags and say they only feel like they’re alive when their boyfriends are inside them. It’s the kind of movie a testicle would make if a testicle made movies and really gave a damn about sound design.

“The Mosquito Bowl” is based on the true story of, if you can believe it, the Mosquito Bowl. A group of Marines played a football game to boost morale on Guadalcanal on Christmas Eve 1944. Several of the men were star players whose careers took a detour after Pearl Harbor, and many of them never made it back home. The Mosquito Bowl was the last football game they ever played.

If there’s one thing I learned from having a dad who was born in the 1940s, it’s that World War II was full of fascinating stories, and almost all of them were interesting enough to fill a double-sized nonfiction book and/or a History Channel miniseries. The fact that an anecdote as juicy as the Mosquito Bowl went overlooked by Hollywood for more than 80 years, even though it’s precisely the type of tale studios have been searching for all this time, is more surprising than anything that actually happens in Berg’s movie.

“The Mosquito Bowl” stars Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgård, Tom Francis and Ray Nicholson as the football-playing heroes. We meet them in the middle of their final games before turning pro, and most of them have recognizable character traits. John McLaughry (Galitzine) is the exception and mostly comes across as the stalwart, emotionally mature man in the group. Bob Baumann (Skarsgård) loves his family and hates Japanese people. Dave Schreiner (Francis) is an overthinker with a chip on his shoulder. Tony Butkovich (Nicholson) has a giant ego but backs it up with real talent.

They find themselves in the same Marine Corps regiment throughout the war. They endure a grueling boot camp, followed by shocking violence on the battlefield. Berg, who co-wrote the screenplay with Mark L. Smith (“The Dog Stars”), doesn’t rush to get to the Mosquito Bowl part of his Mosquito Bowl movie. He takes time to introduce his characters, even though they aren’t presented as deep individuals, so we get the gist right away. items.headline: Netflix cancels Will Ferrell's golf comedy "The Hawk" after one season

items.matters: viewership peaked at 6.2M in week 2 and fell 62% the following week. Budgets were estimated at $5–7M per episode, and the show had 33% from critics on Rotten Tomatoes.
items.body:
Lonnie Hawkins won’t be getting his comeback after all. Netflix has canceled Will Ferrell’s golf comedy The Hawk after just one season, confirming what we’d suspected for some time: the numbers simply didn’t justify the price tag.

The news comes via Deadline, which reports that Netflix has opted not to move forward with a second season. All ten episodes of the series, Ferrell’s first leading role in a TV show, landed on Netflix on July 16th.

As is nearly always the case with Netflix, it comes down to viewership versus cost and the signs have been there for a few weeks now with both Lucas Shaw of Bloomberg and Matt Belloni of Puck have repeatedly been calling it out as one of the streamers big swings that missed in recent months.

On the viewership front, The Hawk was fine but not spectacular. As we covered in our week 1 deep-dive, it opened with 4.8M views, then did something most Netflix comedies don’t by growing in week 2 to 6.2M views, peaking at #2 on the English TV chart. Sadly, the drop-off was steep from there. Week 3 saw hours plunge 62% to just 2.3M views, and it exited the global top 10s entirely after that.

That left the show mid-pack among recent Netflix comedy debuts, which would ordinarily be enough for a renewal. Comedies with smaller launches, like Tires and Leanne, got second seasons.

The problem is that The Hawk wasn’t priced like those shows. Estimates put the budget at $5-7 million per episode, and Deadline adds that Ferrell was commanding a seven-figure salary per episode, making it one of the most expensive comedies on the service. Mid-pack numbers don’t cut it at that price.

Reviews didn’t help, either. Critics were unkind, with the show sitting at 33% on Rotten Tomatoes, although audiences were warmer at 65%.

Regular readers won’t be shocked. In our late 2026 renewal predictions last month, we had The Hawk down as “leaning cancelation,” citing the cost, the weak reviews, and an audience that was almost entirely Western and English-speaking. We also noted that the longer Netflix stayed quiet, the worse the odds got.

There was one glimmer of hope at the time, with a WGA directory listing suggesting some work on a second season was taking place behind the scenes. Evidently, that didn’t amount to anything. The writing was truly on the wall two weeks ago, when co-creator Harper Steele described the show as “short-lived” during an appearance on Late Night with Seth Meyers.

items.headline: "The Night Agent" season 4 will be the final season and is confirmed for 2027
items.summary: production wrapped in Los Angeles, with Gabriel Basso returning and Trevante Rhodes, Elizabeth Lail and Abigail Breslin among the new cast.
items.matters: a Netflix rep called a January 2027 date "inaccurate", and one source floats 24 June 2027, which is unconfirmed.
items.body:
Peter Sutherland returns for one final call in 2027 as Netflix confirms the fourth and final season of the hit thriller has officially wrapped filming.

Peter Sutherland has one last call to answer. Cameras have stopped rolling on the fourth and final season of The Night Agent, Netflix has locked in a 2027 release, and with the cast and all ten episode titles now known, there’s a lot to cover. Here’s everything we know so far about The Night Agent season 4 on Netflix.

Created by Shawn Ryan (The Shield, S.W.A.T.) and based on the novel by Matthew Quirk, The Night Agent debuted in March 2023 and instantly became one of Netflix’s biggest English-language series ever, pulling in over 98 million views in its first 91 days. Three seasons in, the Sony Pictures Television-produced thriller has racked up over 297 million views in total, although as we’ll get into below, each season has been watched noticeably less than the last.

Netflix officially renewed The Night Agent for season 4 on March 6, 2026, just two weeks after season 3 landed, announcing the news with a Times Square stunt and a thank-you from Gabriel Basso.

The renewal had been on the cards for months. Back in November 2025, we reported the show was eyeing an early renewal after season 4 turned up on the California Film Commission’s list of approved projects, and Shawn Ryan later confirmed to Deadline that a writers’ room had been quietly up and running since 2025, with scripts already in hand.

Ryan called the journey so far “a wild ride,” noting that the series had by then shot in five countries across three continents, and said the team was thrilled to keep Peter Sutherland’s adventures going.

Less than two months later, on May 4, 2026, as cameras started rolling, Netflix confirmed that season 4 would be the show’s last, billing it as “One Final Call” for Peter Sutherland.

Ryan put a positive spin on the news, saying he had long wanted to give the series “a proper and thrilling conclusion” and thanking Netflix and Sony Pictures Television for the room to deliver a definitive final season.

Netflix hasn’t given a reason, but the viewing figures are the likely one. Season 3 opened with 8.4 million views, around 40% down on season 2 and 59% down on the show’s premiere. A second-week bump to 9.9 million views helped, but the season faded quickly from there and had slipped to ninth in the English TV chart by its fourth week.

items.headline: Sofia Carson to headline Netflix's NFL Christmas rom-com "The Christmas Game"
items.summary: Laura Terruso directs, and Carson plays a sports agent who must sign her high-school-sweetheart quarterback before Christmas.
items.matters: it is the first narrative feature from Netflix's NFL relationship, shooting 25 January to 4 March 2027 in New Jersey, with a release date not confirmed.
items.body:
Filming is expected to start in the New Year for a possible late 2027 release on Netflix.

Netflix and Sofia Carson are back in business. The streamer has set Carson to lead The Christmas Game, a holiday rom-com made in partnership with the NFL and Skydance Sports Entertainment, with Taylor John Smith and Charlie Hall also signing on. NFL Films is also listed as a production company on the project. Deadline first reported the news.

Laura Terruso is directing. She’s no stranger to Netflix, having helmed the Sabrina Carpenter dance comedy Work It back in 2020, and most recently directed Lionsgate’s About My Father. The script comes from Danielle Morrow and Vanessa Marano, who know this territory well, having written Hallmark’s NFL romances Holiday Touchdown: A Bills Love Story and A Make or Break Holiday.

Carson plays a blunt, high-flying sports agent who gets publicly dumped by her star client. To save her job, she has to land an even bigger name before Christmas: an elite NFL quarterback who happens to be her high school sweetheart. Standing in her way is a ruthless rival agent who’ll do whatever it takes to sign him first. Smith and Hall round out the love triangle.

Jesse Sisgold, Jason Reed, and Sandino Moya Smith are producing for Skydance Sports Entertainment, with Carson and Jessica Matthews serving as executive producers.

Netflix has streamed NFL games on Christmas Day since 2024, but this is the first narrative feature to come out of the relationship. It’s a logical extension of the brand, and Hallmark has already shown there’s an audience for football-flavored festive romance.

The timing isn’t a coincidence either. Netflix’s holiday rom-coms keep delivering, with Leighton Meester and Jared Padalecki’s Guarding Stars just pulling in 27.6 million views in its first three days.

We can add that production is currently scheduled to run from January 25th to March 4th, 2027, in New Jersey. Dominika Posseren is the casting director. That schedule lines up with a holiday 2027 release, although Netflix has yet to confirm a date.

Taylor John Smith is best known for Where the Crawdads Sing, Warfare, and HBO’s Sharp Objects. Charlie Hall stars opposite Tatiana Maslany in Apple’s Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed, will appear in The White Lotus season 4, and is writing and starring in a college fraternity drug ring series for Netflix, executive produced by Barry ‘s Alec Berg.

items.headline: "One Last Shot" sets a 22 December Netflix US debut
items.summary: Scott Adkins and Dolph Lundgren star in James Nunn's finale to the one-take action trilogy, set just hours after "One More Shot".
items.matters: like its predecessors, it is presented as one continuous real-time shot, including an ATV chase and a boat sequence.
items.body:
The third and final One Shot movie, with Dolph Lundgren joining the fight, lands on Netflix US on December 22nd, 2026.

Netflix’s steady supply of Sony Pictures action movies continues into the holidays. One Last Shot, the closing chapter of James Nunn and Scott Adkins’ single-take action trilogy, will make its SVOD debut on Netflix in the United States on December 22nd, 2026. Here’s everything you need to know.

It’s the second movie in the series to make its streaming debut on Netflix, following One More Shot, which arrived in May 2024.

Picking up just hours after the events of One More Shot, the threequel throws Navy SEAL Jake Harris straight back into the fire. Following a dirty bomb attack on the State of the Union, the Joint Chiefs are moved to a secure compound, which is promptly seized by a team of mercenaries looking to take control of the US missile defense network.

Leading them is Elliot Carter, a disillusioned former comrade who once took a bullet for Harris. Harris is drafted onto the assault team by Admiral Mulholland, who quietly orders him to take Carter out.

As with the first two movies, the big hook is the format: the action plays out in real time and is presented as one continuous shot. This time, that includes an ATV chase and a boat sequence.

Scott Adkins returns as Jake Harris, capping a busy year on Netflix for the British action star, who also featured in Matt Damon and Ben Affleck’s The Rip back in January.

Behind the camera, James Nunn directs for the third time, working from a script by series writer Jamie Russell. Austin Wintory returns to score, and Tim Man handles the fight choreography. Filming took place in west London in late 2025.

The movie skipped theaters in the US, with Sony Pictures Home Entertainment releasing it on digital and DVD on September 22nd. That puts its Netflix debut exactly three months later.

It arrives through Netflix’s first window deal with Sony Pictures, which doesn’t just cover the studio’s big theatrical releases. It also takes in Sony’s direct-to-video slate, which is how Sniper: No Nation arrived over the summer.

Not for now. In the UK and Ireland, the movie is a Sky Original and is available on Sky Cinema. Elsewhere, Sony’s global Pay-1 deal with Netflix doesn’t kick in until 2027.

One More Shot made little noise on its VOD release in January 2024, but found a second life on Netflix, climbing as high as number four in the US movie top 10s. With Lundgren’s name on the poster and a release date in the middle of the holiday break, the finale has a decent shot at going one…

items.headline: Commission proposes the Digital Fairness Act
items.summary: adopted on 11 November, it would replace the 2005 Unfair Commercial Practices Directive with a regulation that applies directly in all 27 states. It bans dark patterns, requires renewal reminders and online cancellation in a few clicks, and bans paid loot boxes for under-18s.
items.matters: it covers any trader targeting EU consumers, with fines up to 6% of global turnover. Subscription flows, pre-ticked boxes, urgency pop-ups and in-game currency display would all need redesign, though years of negotiation lie ahead.
items.body:
The proposal would also let adults switch off addictive features and end subscription traps, with fines of up to 6% of global turnover.

The European Commission proposed today the Digital Fairness Act, a consumer rulebook that would ban loot boxes for minors, blacklist manipulative interface design, and put a termination button on every online subscription.

The proposal would repeal the EU’s 2005 Unfair Commercial Practices Directive and replace it with a directly applicable regulation, swapping 27 national rulebooks for one. Any trader targeting EU consumers falls in scope, wherever it is based.

Dark patterns get a general prohibition plus an annex of practices banned in all circumstances, a list the Commission can extend without reopening the law. Euronews, which reviewed the text ahead of publication, counts ten blacklisted traps, from false low-stock claims to pre-ticked add-ons and nagging pop-ups.

Gaming takes the hardest hit. In-game currencies must display their real-money value and stay off by default for minors unless a parent approves.

Paid loot boxes must disclose their odds, are banned for under-18s outright, and every player, adult or not, gets the option to disable them. Pay-to-win and pay-to-progress mechanics are also off limits for minors.

Adults get something rarer: an off switch. Services must let users disable features designed, or reasonably foreseen, to encourage compulsive use, the same design question Brussels is already probing in its Snapchat proceedings.

Subscriptions round out the list. Free trials cannot quietly roll into paid plans without active acceptance, renewals come with reminders, cancelling must work online in a few clicks, and consumers keep a right to reach a human.

The EU has fought this fight before, one Prime cancellation at a time; now the fix would be structural.

Enforcement moves closer to Brussels too. A parallel revision of the consumer protection cooperation rules would let the Commission investigate major cross-border infringements itself, with fines of up to 6% of global turnover, per Euronews.

The Commission’s impact assessment weighs an estimated €88.4B in reduced consumer detriment over a decade against adjusted business costs of €678M a year.

The proposal now heads to the European Parliament and member states, where the fights over protecting minors online are already well rehearsed. Years of negotiation lie ahead, but the direction is set: the design tricks that built the attention economy are becoming illegal terrain in Europe.

items.headline: Commission preliminarily finds Temu in breach of the DSA over illegal products
items.summary: published 17 November, it cites ineffective product-compliance checks, a weak content moderation system and an ineffective sanction system.
items.matters: these are preliminary findings only, and the page gives no fine. It comes while Temu's interim risk assessment under its earlier remedy plan is due 30 November, so scrutiny of marketplace compliance is stacking up.
items.body:
The European Commission preliminarily found Temu in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA) obligation to put in place reasonable, proportionate and effective measures to mitigate the risk of illegal products being offered on its platform.

The Commission preliminarily found that Temu's mitigation measures include ineffective controls to check the compliance of products; a weak content moderation system; and an ineffective sanction system.

Shopping online should not mean risking the purchase of illegal and unsafe products. Under the Digital Services Act, platforms are responsible for protecting users from the risk of illegal content and goods. The preliminary findings against Temu mark another step towards making the online world safer.

items.headline: Commission preliminarily finds TikTok's "For You" feed in breach of the DSA
items.summary: the 6 November findings say the recommender's "rabbit hole" effect can harm mental health, and focus on both risk assessment and mitigation.
items.matters: if you ship a recommender on a large platform, the Commission treats engagement-driven feedback loops as a systemic risk to assess and mitigate, not just a design choice.
items.body:
The European Commission has preliminarily found TikTok in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA) for the so-called ‘rabbit hole effect’ of its recommender system.

TikTok's ‘For You' feed shows users a continuous stream of personalised videos, even when those are related to mental health struggles and body image.

The more a user interacts with a certain type of content, the more TikTok's ‘For You' feed algorithm recommends similar content. This design can be harmful when such endless and repeated exposure involves, for example, content about sadness, isolation or body image. These ‘rabbit holes' can have a detrimental impact on users' mental health, especially that of vulnerable adults and minors.

items.headline: FIA confirms Williams overspent the 2025 cost cap, Alpine guilty of a procedural breach
items.summary: Williams exceeded the limit by £627,000 (0.48%), which the FIA classed as a minor overspend and procedural breach, and the penalty is an undisclosed fine plus a 1.5% cut to wind tunnel and CFD allowances.
items.matters: Williams' wind tunnel runs drop from 336 to 331 hours this period and from 352 to 347 in the first half of 2027, while Alpine, which did not overspend, gets only a fine over wrongly excluded marketing and HR costs.
items.body:
The FIA have completed their review of the F1 teams' and power unit manufacturers' compliance with the 2025 Financial Regulations.

Formula 1's governing body the FIA have completed their review of the F1 teams’ and power unit manufacturers’ compliance with the 2025 Financial Regulations, with Williams found to have committed an unintentional minor overspend breach and a procedural breach, while Alpine also made a procedural breach.

As part of the review by the Cost Cap Administration (CCA) – a process that took eight months – all 11 Formula 1 teams and all five power unit (PU) manufacturers submitted financial documentation from 2025.

Nine of the 11 teams and all five power unit manufacturers were found in compliance for 2025, but Williams were found to have unintentionally committed a minor overspend breach and a procedural breach.

In a document confirming that an Accepted Breach Agreement (ABA) has been entered into between Williams and the Cost Cap Administration, it was explained that “there is no evidence that WGPE [Williams Grand Prix Engineering] gained or sought to gain any advantage (sporting or otherwise) from the identified breaches”, and that “the minor overspend breach amounts to £627k and therefore, with 0.48% over the 2025 Cost Cap, falls at the lower end of the <5% minor overspend range”.

Williams will subsequently pay a financial penalty for the breach, as well as taking a 1.5% reduction in wind tunnel and CFD testing over the next 12 months.

The team said in a statement: “The breach relates to administrative costs we incurred making changes to our company structure. We believed these costs fell outside of the cap. Following discussions with the FIA, we have agreed to resolve the matter in line with their interpretation that the costs should have been in cap.

“The FIA has noted that Williams did not gain any sporting or financial advantage, and nor did we ever seek to. It has also noted that we acted cooperatively and in good faith throughout the review process.

A procedural breach was identified for Alpine, with the FIA confirming that “there is no evidence that Alpine gained or sought to gain any advantage from the inaccurate exclusions or adjustments of certain costs; and notwithstanding the Cost Cap Administration’s determination of procedural breach, Alpine’s relevant costs in respect of the 2025 Reporting Period were below the 2025 Cost Cap”.

Fresh from one of the most exciting races in recent memory, it’s time to shift focus to the Gulf for the final two rounds of the 2026 season. There wasn’t only great racing to talk about after Las Vegas, but frustrations and controversies among teams and drivers that could still be simmering under the surface as we make the trip to Qatar.

Tensions rose in Las Vegas during the final practice session of the weekend, particularly between Max Verstappen and George Russell.

With the first two sessions impacted by rain, and no dry running possible, FP3 was a busy session with drivers looking to get as much data as they could before locking in their set-ups ahead of qualifying. That led to a moment where Russell and Verstappen fought on track, and Russell later spoke out against the Dutchman's approach.

The pair started alongside each other on the front row and delivered a thrilling fight in a remarkable race until Russell hit the barrier trying to overtake team mate Kimi Antonelli, with Verstappen going on to secure his fourth victory in six races.

Qatar was the scene of a disagreement between the two drivers back in 2024, after Verstappen was given a grid penalty for impeding Russell during Qualifying. Verstappen said he “lost all respect” for Russell following the stewards’ hearing, and they now return to the scene of that incident after another verbal joust.

items.headline: Alonso: Aston Martin "can't be competitive" with the Honda power unit
items.summary: he said on the team's website that the AMR26 was 33 km/h slower than the fastest car in qualifying and loses more than two seconds a lap on the straights in Las Vegas.
items.matters: Honda's upgrade added horsepower but hurt driveability, and Alonso says he is encouraged by the factory work and confident about 2027.
items.body:
Fernando Alonso says Honda is “a very long way behind” its Formula 1 rivals and Aston Martin therefore “can’t be competitive” with the Japanese engine, albeit expressing hope for the future.

As F1 switched to power units featuring 47% electrical energy, Honda’s new powertrain has been lacking both power and reliability. The ADUO upgrade introduced by the manufacturer at the Dutch Grand Prix improved its horsepower output at the expense of driveability, which had been a problem from the start with what Alonso described as “random downshifts”.

Lance Stroll suffered his 13th race retirement of the season in Brazil due to an ERS issue, with the situation so dire that Honda saw the near double finish in Las Vegas – Alonso retired before the last lap – as encouraging, despite the green cars only leading Valtteri Bottas ’ Cadillac at the end of the race.

The high-speed layout didn’t help as Honda remains noticeably down on power, with the AMR26 33km/h slower than the fastest car in qualifying, while its straightline deficit was 27km/h in the race.

“On the engine side, we are a very long way behind and we can't be competitive with the power unit we have,” Alonso admitted on the Aston Martin website.

“There are some circuits like Las Vegas where we are losing more than two seconds a lap on the straights alone, and the reliability is not where it needs to be. No one is happy with how things are going on the PU side of things, but we know Honda is working hard to improve the situation.

On the chassis side however, progress meant Alonso managed to finish ninth on the winding Zandvoort track and eighth in Sepang’s wet conditions – two contexts in which the power deficit wasn’t as impactful.

“The Budapest chassis upgrade was supposed to deliver a certain lap time, and it delivered that lap time,” Alonso said. “We were competitive in Budapest and we scored points in Zandvoort and Malaysia.

items.headline: Aeon on how El Niño became a global threat
items.summary: Dagomar Degroot's essay (23 November, about 4,100 words) argues that El Niño's human toll has depended more on power and exploitation shaping vulnerability than on the strength of the weather. As I write these words, surface water temperatures across a great swath of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean have been rising for months. El Niño is the name for the recurring and sustained warming of this part of the Pacific. And temperatures are soaring to such highs, relative to their long-term averages, that the El Niño of 2026 may be the strongest in 1,000 years.

It’s still uncertain how the warming ocean will reshape global weather in the months to come, let alone how ecosystems – and human populations – will respond. The future is always murky. Still, when it comes to El Niño, the past could teach us what to expect. And not just the recent past, but also the deep past recently recovered by scientists, historians and archaeologists.

I’m an environmental historian. I work with climatologists to understand how climates have changed in the past. I study how communities understood and adapted to the climate’s changes. And my research suggests that history can help us understand even the most extreme events in today’s rapidly warming climate.

The past can help us see why El Niño is so hard to forecast, for example, or even define. It can show us that, while El Niño has contributed to the deaths of millions of people in the past, it has also enabled others to amass wealth and power.

El Niño indisputably scrambles worldwide weather patterns, but history teaches us that it’s as much a human creation as a natural reality. And this context may help us weather not only the effects of the 2026-27 El Niño in the months to come, but also El Niño ’s future on a warming planet.

A vast current of cold water snakes up the western coast of South America. In December each year, that current breaks down for about a month. An influx of warm water delivers tropical fish and – because warm water evaporates more readily than cold water – abundant rainfall.

It’s impossible to know when people first noticed this annual reversal of water temperatures and precipitation. We do know that, sometime after the 16th-century Spanish conquest of the Inka Empire, fishermen named it El Niño, meaning literally ‘the boy’ or, when capitalised, ‘The Christ Child’. At least the reason for the name seems clear: the reversal of current happens around Christmas.

The colonised heartland of the Inka Empire, now known as Peru, won its independence in the 19th century. Towards the end of that century, Peru’s government joined many of its counterparts by establishing a society of geographers to describe the country’s environment and to catalogue its resources.
